question: What is the difference between let and var in Swift?
answer:
A `let` binding can be assigned exactly once; a `var` binding can be reassigned as often as you like.

• let — the binding is fixed after initialization. Initialization can still be deferred, so `let x: Int; if c { x = 1 } else { x = 2 }` is legal.
• var — the binding can be pointed at a new value at any time.

The interesting part is how this interacts with value and reference semantics:
• For a value type (struct, enum) `let` freezes the whole value — you cannot mutate its stored properties or call a `mutating` method on it.
• For a reference type (class) `let` freezes only the reference — the object's own `var` properties are still settable through it.

Idiomatic Swift is `let` by default; the compiler emits a warning when a `var` is never mutated. It is not only style: a final class whose stored properties are all `let` of Sendable type gets `Sendable` conformance for free, which matters as soon as the value crosses an actor boundary.

question: What are optionals in Swift and how do you safely unwrap them?
answer:
An optional makes "this value might be missing" part of the type instead of a runtime surprise.

Under the hood `Optional<T>` is an enum with two cases, `.some(T)` and `.none`, which you write in source as `T?`.

Safe unwrapping options:
• `if let` / `guard let` — bind only when non-nil; the shorthand `guard let name else` reuses the same name
• `??` — nil-coalescing default
• `?.` — optional chaining, propagates nil through the whole expression
• `map` / `flatMap` — transform the wrapped value without unwrapping
• `switch` on `.some` / `.none` when you want both branches explicit

Force-unwrapping with `!` traps on nil. Reserve it for cases that are genuinely unreachable — a hardcoded URL literal, an outlet the storyboard guarantees — and write a real error path everywhere else. `try!` and implicitly unwrapped optionals (`String!`) carry the same risk.

question: Explain value types vs reference types in Swift.
answer:
Swift divides every type into value types, which are copied when you assign or pass them, and reference types, which are shared.

• Value types — struct, enum, tuple. Each variable owns its own copy, so nobody else can mutate it behind your back. That is what makes them the safe default under strict concurrency.
• Reference types — class, actor, closure. Many variables can point at one instance, and a mutation through any of them is visible to all.

Apple's guidance is to reach for `struct` first and use `class` only when you need something a value cannot give you: stable identity (`===`), inheritance, `deinit`, or Objective-C bridging.

The standard library collections — Array, Dictionary, Set, String — are all value types with copy-on-write. The buffer is shared until someone writes to it, so a copy costs a retain, not a memcpy. `isKnownUniquelyReferenced` is how you implement the same trick in your own types.

question: What are closures in Swift and how do capture lists work?
answer:
Closures are self-contained blocks of functionality (named or anonymous) that can be passed around. They capture variables from their surrounding scope by reference (for reference types) or by copying (for value types).

A capture list `[weak self]` / `[unowned self]` lets you opt into different memory semantics — required to avoid retain cycles when a closure outlives its owner (e.g. stored on a view, networking layer, or NotificationCenter).

Trailing-closure syntax + shorthand parameters ($0, $1) make Swift closures concise.

question: What is the difference between Array, Set, and Dictionary in Swift?
answer:
Array, Set and Dictionary are the three standard-library collections, and choosing between them is really a choice about ordering and lookup cost.

• `Array<Element>` — ordered and index-addressed, duplicates allowed. O(1) random access, amortised O(1) append, but O(n) for `contains`.
• `Set<Element>` — unordered and unique; `Element` must be `Hashable`. O(1) average insert and `contains`, plus union/intersection/subtracting.
• `Dictionary<Key, Value>` — unordered key-to-value pairs with unique `Hashable` keys. O(1) average lookup.

All three are value types with copy-on-write, so passing one around is cheap until somebody mutates it.

All three also conform to Sequence and Collection, so `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `sorted` and `first(where:)` work identically on each — which is why the right answer to "my `contains` is slow in a loop" is usually "turn the Array into a Set first".

question: Explain Swift error handling: throws, try, do/catch, Result.
answer:
Swift makes failure part of a function's signature: a function that can fail is marked `throws` and every caller must write `try`.

Errors are ordinary values conforming to the `Error` protocol, and an enum with associated values is the usual shape — it lets the caller `switch` on the exact failure and pull out a retry delay or a field name.

Forms of try:
• `try` — propagate the error to the caller
• `try?` — collapse to an Optional, discarding the error
• `try!` — trap on error; same risk profile as force-unwrapping

`do` / `catch` handles the error locally, and `catch` patterns can match specific cases. When you need to store an outcome rather than handle it immediately — caching, passing across a boundary, testing — use `Result<Success, Failure>`.

Typed throws (`func f() throws(AuthError)`) landed in Swift 6: the compiler then knows the exact error type, so `catch` is exhaustive and no `as?` cast is needed. Untyped `throws` is still the default and still right for most APIs, because adding a new error case to a typed throws function is a source-breaking change.

question: Swift has tuples, ranges and `guard` — what problem does each one solve?
answer:
Tuples, ranges and `guard` are three small features that turn up in almost every Swift file, and each one replaces something heavier.

• Tuple — a fixed-size group of typed, optionally named values. It buys you a multi-value return without declaring a struct: `func minMax(_ xs: [Int]) -> (min: Int, max: Int)?`. The moment the tuple escapes the function it was made in, or needs a method, promote it to a struct.
• Range — `0..<10` is half-open, `1...10` is closed, and one-sided forms like `2...` and `...2` slice collections. Ranges conform to Sequence, so you iterate them directly and use them as subscripts into arrays and strings.
• guard — an early exit that the compiler forces you to honour: the `else` block must leave the current scope. Unlike `if let`, the bound value stays in scope for the rest of the function, so the happy path stays flat and unindented instead of drifting right with every nested check.

The rule of thumb for `guard` versus `if let`: use `guard` when the nil case means "we're done here", and `if let` when the nil case is just another branch you want to handle.
